ox: Incorrect. 0.83 is 1000/1200, the ratio upside down. Specific gravity is the substance's density divided by water's density, with the substance on top.
Correct. SG = ρ(substance) / ρ(water) = 1200 / 1000 = 1.2. Units cancel, so SG has none.
Incorrect. 1200 is the density in kg/m³, not the ratio to water. You still have to divide by 1000.
Incorrect. 1.2 is the right number but the units are wrong. A ratio of two densities has no units, so 'kg/m³' cannot be attached.

p: Specific gravity compares a substance's density to the density of water (1000 kg/m³, or 1 g/cm³). Because it is a ratio of two densities, it has no units. A value above 1 means the substance is denser than water and sinks in it; below 1 it floats.

x4B_001.trap: Reporting 1200, or attaching the units kg/m³; specific gravity is a pure ratio.
x4B_001.eli: Specific gravity is a 'how many times heavier than water' score for the same size of cup.
mem: Water: 1000 kg/m³ = 1 g/cm³.
SG has NO units.
SG > 1 sinks in water; SG < 1 floats.

fm.f: SG = ρ_substance / ρ_water, where ρ_substance = density of the saline (1200 kg/m³), ρ_water = density of water (1000 kg/m³)
fm.why: We divide by water's density because specific gravity is defined as a ratio against water.

ox: Incorrect. Oxygen content does not change how fast a liquid flows through a tube. The question is about fluid flow, which depends on pressure, radius, length and viscosity.
Incorrect. Radius is unchanged, but viscosity is NOT unchanged. More red cells make blood thicker, so flow changes even though radius stays the same.
Correct. Poiseuille: Q = ΔP·πr⁴ / (8ηL). ΔP, r and L stay the same, but η (viscosity) rises with hematocrit, so Q falls. Thicker blood is harder to push.
Incorrect. Density plays no role in Poiseuille flow. Viscosity (resistance to flow), not density (mass per volume), is what rises with more red cells.

p: Poiseuille's law gives the flow rate of a viscous fluid through a tube: Q = ΔP·πr⁴ / (8ηL). Flow rises with pressure difference and with radius to the FOURTH power, and falls with viscosity and length. Blood viscosity rises with hematocrit, which is why polycythemia makes blood harder to move.

d_4B_12.trap: Thinking more red cells means more flow because more oxygen is carried. Flow rate here is fluid mechanics, not oxygen delivery.
d_4B_12.eli: Blood with more red cells is like switching from water to syrup: it pours more slowly through the same straw.
mem: Poiseuille: Q = ΔP·πr⁴ / (8ηL).
Flow ∝ r⁴ (a tiny change in radius matters a lot) and ∝ 1/η.
Higher hematocrit → higher viscosity → lower flow.

fm.f: Q = ΔP·π·r⁴ / (8·η·L), where Q = flow rate, ΔP = pressure difference, r = vessel radius, η = viscosity, L = vessel length
fm.v: ΔP, r and L unchanged; η goes UP
fm.s: Q ∝ 1/η, so if η doubles then Q is cut in half
fm.why: We use Poiseuille's law because it tells us how each property of the vessel and the fluid changes flow.

d_4B_12.sc: Change one variable at a time: with pressure and tube fixed, flow moves opposite to viscosity.
d_4B_12.mn: Radius to the Fourth power rules the tube; viscosity is the enemy: thicker = slower.

ox: Correct. Myoglobin has ONE heme and no cooperativity, so its curve is a hyperbola. Its P50 is about 2 mmHg, so it holds O₂ tightly even at very low PO₂ (higher affinity than hemoglobin).
Incorrect. A sigmoidal curve with lower affinity describes HEMOGLOBIN (4 subunits, cooperative, P50 ≈ 26 mmHg), not myoglobin.
Incorrect. Myoglobin does have higher affinity, but a sigmoidal curve requires cooperativity between subunits. Myoglobin has just one, so its curve cannot be sigmoidal.
Incorrect. Hyperbolic is right, but lower affinity is wrong. A P50 of about 2 mmHg is much lower than hemoglobin's 26 mmHg, which means HIGHER affinity.

p: Hemoglobin has four subunits that help each other (cooperativity), giving an S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve with P50 ≈ 26 mmHg. Myoglobin has one subunit, so it simply binds O₂ with a hyperbolic curve and P50 ≈ 2 mmHg. Lower P50 = higher affinity: myoglobin stores O₂ in muscle and releases it only when PO₂ is very low.

d_4B_10.trap: Assuming the sigmoidal curve belongs to the protein with the higher affinity.
d_4B_10.eli: Myoglobin is a warehouse that holds on tight to oxygen; hemoglobin is a delivery truck that drops it off where tissues need it.
mem: Mb: 1 heme, hyperbolic, P50 ≈ 2 mmHg, stores O₂ in muscle.
Hb: 4 hemes, sigmoidal, P50 ≈ 26 mmHg, delivers O₂.
Lower P50 = higher affinity = curve further LEFT.
d_4B_10.sc: Smaller P50 means it grabs O₂ harder, so its curve sits further to the left.
d_4B_10.mn: Mb = Muscle bank (stores O₂). Hb = Hauls and hands off O₂.

ox: Correct. In a narrowed segment the same flow squeezes through a smaller area, so the blood speeds up (continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂). Bernoulli then says that in a horizontal vessel faster flow goes with LOWER pressure.
Incorrect. Faster flow does NOT come with higher pressure. In a horizontal tube, kinetic energy per volume (½ρv²) rises at the expense of pressure.
Incorrect. The narrowing makes blood go FASTER, not slower. Slower flow would happen where the vessel widens.
Incorrect. Pressure is lower, but velocity is not. Both must be considered together: narrow → fast → low pressure.

concept.t: Continuity and Bernoulli in a narrowed vessel
p: The continuity equation says that the volume of fluid passing each point per second is constant: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. A smaller cross-section A means a larger speed v. Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal tube, P + ½ρv² = constant, then says that higher speed means lower pressure.

d_4B_3.trap: Thinking that a narrowing raises pressure because it feels 'squeezed'. Static pressure in the narrow, fast part is actually lower.
d_4B_3.eli: Think of a garden hose: pinch the end and the water shoots out faster. The fast water has less 'push sideways' on the walls, so its pressure is lower.
mem: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ (narrow → fast).
Bernoulli (horizontal): P + ½ρv² = constant (fast → low pressure).
Narrow = Fast = Low pressure (in a horizontal tube).

fm.f: A₁·v₁ = A₂·v₂, where A = cross-sectional area of the vessel, v = speed of the blood; subscript 1 = normal segment, 2 = narrowed segment
fm.v: Say the narrow segment has half the area: A₂ = ½A₁, and v₁ = 1 (any unit)
fm.s: A₁·1 = ½A₁·v₂ → v₂ = 2. Speed doubles; then P + ½ρv² constant means P drops
fm.why: We use continuity first because it tells us how the speed changes; Bernoulli then converts that speed change into a pressure change.

d_4B_3.sc: Area down → speed up (continuity). Speed up → pressure down (Bernoulli). Two steps, no numbers needed.
d_4B_3.mn: Narrow = Fast = Low: N-F-L, like the 'NFL' of fluids.

ox: One capillary is narrow, but there are billions in parallel. Velocity depends on the total area they add up to, which is huge, so velocity falls.
Pressure drops steadily from aorta to veins, so it is not constant. And velocity is set by continuity, not by constant pressure.
Capillary resistance is high, but that lowers pressure. Speed is governed by total cross-sectional area, not resistance.
Correct. Continuity says A1 v1 = A2 v2. If total area is 1000 times larger, velocity is about 1000 times lower. Slow flow gives time for exchange.

p: Continuity says that the flow rate (volume per second) is the same all along the circuit: area times velocity is constant. Cross-sectional area is the size of the opening that blood flows through.
Capillaries are tiny, but together they have a far larger total area than the aorta. So blood slows down there, which gives time for oxygen and nutrients to move into tissues.

d_4B_1.eli: A river squeezed into one narrow channel rushes. When it spreads into a wide marsh, the water barely moves.
mem: A x v = constant (flow rate).
Total capillary area is largest, so velocity is lowest.
Aorta has highest velocity; capillaries lowest.

fm.f: A1 x v1 = A2 x v2, where A = total cross-sectional area, v = velocity
fm.why: Blood is incompressible, so flow rate is the same at each level.
fm.nc: Cancel A1 on both sides.

d_4B_1.trap: Looking at one capillary's tiny radius instead of the total area of all capillaries in parallel.

ox: Oxygen is carried by blood, bound to hemoglobin. Lymph vessels do not transport oxygen to tissues.
Lymph does not directly raise capillary oncotic pressure (the pull of plasma proteins). Returning protein only helps indirectly.
Correct. Capillaries filter out more fluid than they take back. Lymph collects the extra fluid and leaked protein and returns it to the veins.
Lymphatic vessels start in the tissue spaces (interstitium), not at arterioles.

p: Capillaries leak fluid into tissue spaces (filtration) and take some back (reabsorption). More leaves than returns. The interstitium is the space between cells.
The lymphatic system is a one-way drain. It collects the extra fluid (lymph) and protein and returns them to veins. Without it, tissues swell (edema).

d_4B_17.eli: A sink with a faucet slightly faster than the drain overflows. Lymph vessels are an extra drain that keeps the floor dry.
mem: Filtration exceeds reabsorption; lymph returns the surplus.
Lymph also returns protein that leaked out.
Blocked lymph causes edema.
d_4B_17.trap: Forgetting that capillaries filter more than they reabsorb, which is why a drain is needed.
d_4B_17.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. For a sphere, Laplace's law gives P = 2T/r. Smaller radius gives higher pressure, so small alveoli push air into big ones unless surfactant lowers T.
Wall tension is not directly proportional to radius here. For alveoli, the pressure is inversely related to radius. T = Pr is the vessel form, not the alveolar one.
Small alveoli have lower compliance (stiffer), not greater, because of their higher collapsing pressure.
Large alveoli do not have higher surface tension. The problem is that pressure is highest in the small ones.

p: Alveoli are tiny air sacs in the lungs. Water on their lining creates surface tension, a force that tries to shrink them. Laplace's law for a sphere: P = 2T/r, where P is the pressure pushing inward, T is surface tension and r is radius.
Smaller r means higher P, so small alveoli empty into large ones. Surfactant is a soapy substance that lowers T, which keeps the sacs open.

d_4B_18.eli: Connect a small balloon and a big balloon. The small one has more squeeze pressure and empties into the big one.
mem: Alveolus: P = 2T/r.
Smaller alveolus has higher pressure.
Surfactant lowers surface tension and prevents collapse.
d_4B_18.trap: Using the vessel wall-tension form T = Pr and picking 'tension proportional to radius'.
d_4B_18.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Contracting the diaphragm makes the chest bigger, not smaller. Trap: if pressure rose, air would be pushed out, which is expiration.
Correct. The diaphragm flattens and the chest volume goes up. By Boyle's law (P x V is constant), more volume means lower pressure. Lung pressure drops below atmospheric, so air flows in.
Wrong. Pressure above atmospheric pushes air out of the lungs. That is what happens in expiration. Do not mix up the two directions.
Wrong. Lung tissue has no muscle to pull air. It is passive and follows the chest wall. Trap: thinking breathing is the lungs sucking, not a pressure gradient.

p: Air always moves from high pressure to low pressure. Boyle's law says that for a gas, pressure and volume are inversely related: bigger space, lower pressure.
The diaphragm is the dome-shaped muscle under the lungs. When it contracts it flattens, the chest gets bigger, lung pressure falls below the air outside, and air rushes in.

d_4B_19.eli: Pull the plunger of a syringe back. The space gets bigger, the pressure drops, and air rushes in to fill it.
mem: Inspiration: diaphragm contracts, chest volume up, lung pressure down, air in
Expiration is passive at rest: volume down, pressure up, air out
Boyle's law: P x V = constant (inverse)

fm.f: P1 x V1 = P2 x V2, where P = gas pressure, V = gas volume (temperature and amount of gas constant)
fm.v: V2 is greater than V1 during inspiration
fm.s: If V doubles, P is cut in half; so P2 < P1 and falls below atmospheric
fm.why: Boyle's law links the volume change of the chest to the pressure change inside it.
fm.nc: No numbers needed; just say bigger volume means smaller pressure.

d_4B_19.trap: Believing inspiration is the body pushing air in. It is a pressure gradient created by a volume change.
d_4B_19.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Fibrosis scars the lung and does not add surface area. If anything, area is lost. Trap: picking the answer that sounds like more tissue means more exchange.
Wrong. Fick's law has thickness in it, so a thicker wall changes the rate even if partial pressures stay the same. Trap: only looking at the pressure gradient.
Wrong. Tissue density is not a term in Fick's law. Denser, thicker tissue does not speed diffusion.
Correct. Fick's law: rate is proportional to area x pressure difference, divided by thickness. Thicker walls mean a longer path, so diffusion slows.

p: Diffusion is the spontaneous spread of molecules from high to low concentration. Fick's law says the rate goes up with more surface area and a bigger pressure difference, and goes down with a longer distance.
In pulmonary fibrosis the walls between air and blood become scarred and thick. Gases must travel farther, so exchange is slower.

d_4B_20.eli: Shouting through a thin curtain is easy to hear. Shouting through a thick brick wall is hard.
mem: Rate = (area x pressure difference) / thickness
Thicker membrane lowers diffusion
Fibrosis and edema both thicken the barrier; emphysema lowers area

fm.f: Rate is proportional to (A x dP) / d, where A = surface area, dP = partial pressure difference, d = membrane thickness
fm.v: d doubles; A and dP unchanged
fm.s: Rate is proportional to 1/2, so it falls by half
fm.why: Thickness is in the denominator, so thicker means slower.
fm.nc: Just compare factors: bigger d gives a smaller rate.

d_4B_20.trap: Forgetting that thickness is in the denominator of Fick's law.
d_4B_20.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. This is the Haldane effect. When hemoglobin gives up O2 in the tissues, it binds more CO2 and H+. That helps carry CO2 away from the tissues.
Wrong. Oxygen release goes with CO2 pickup, not CO2 release. CO2 is released in the lungs, where hemoglobin picks up oxygen.
Wrong. A left shift means higher oxygen affinity, which would hurt unloading. Also, this is not what the Haldane effect describes.
Wrong. CO2 and H+ binding actually help unload oxygen. That is the Bohr effect, the reverse relationship.

p: Hemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. When it has let go of oxygen (deoxygenated), it holds on to CO2 and H+ more tightly.
In the tissues, oxygen leaves and CO2 enters the blood, and deoxygenated hemoglobin helps carry it. In the lungs the opposite happens.

d_4B_23.eli: A backpack that is empty has room, so it picks up trash on the way. Once it is full of lunch, it drops the trash.
mem: Haldane: less O2 on Hb means more CO2 and H+ binding
Bohr: more CO2 and H+ means less O2 affinity (right shift)
Tissues: O2 off, CO2 on. Lungs: O2 on, CO2 off
d_4B_23.trap: Mixing up the Haldane effect (O2 level changes CO2 binding) with the Bohr effect (CO2 and H+ change O2 binding).
d_4B_23.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. A heavier molecule diffuses more slowly, not faster. Solubility is the main factor here.
Correct. Diffusion depends on the gradient and on how well the gas dissolves in the membrane and plasma. CO2 is about 20 times more soluble than O2, which makes up for its small gradient.
Wrong. Hemoglobin binding does not drive crossing the alveolar membrane. Most CO2 travels as bicarbonate, not bound to hemoglobin.
Wrong. CO2 crosses by passive diffusion. No pump is used in gas exchange.

p: How fast a gas crosses a membrane depends on its pressure gradient and on its solubility, meaning how well it dissolves in water and membrane.
CO2 has only a small gradient (about 6 mmHg), but it dissolves about 20 times better than O2. Both effects together give fast diffusion.

d_4B_32.eli: A small hill with a super slippery slide can still get you down fast.
mem: CO2 is about 20x more soluble than O2
Diffusion rate depends on gradient and solubility
Gas exchange is passive
d_4B_32.trap: Assuming a small gradient must mean slow diffusion.
d_4B_32.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Veins have thin walls with little muscle. Thick muscular walls describe arteries. Trap: giving veins artery features.
Correct. Veins have one-way valves that stop blood from sliding back down. Squeezing of leg muscles (the skeletal muscle pump) pushes blood up toward the heart through those valves.
Wrong. High pressure in leg veins from gravity makes blood pool. It does not stop backflow.
Wrong. Capillary flow is smooth, not pulsing. The pulse is damped before blood reaches capillaries.

p: Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure. They are thin and stretchy, so they hold most of the body's blood volume.
Because blood in the legs must go uphill, veins have one-way valves. When leg muscles contract, they squeeze the veins and push blood up. The valves stop it falling back.

d_4B_37.eli: Like a ladder you climb with a gate on each rung that only swings up: you can go up but never slide back.
mem: Veins: thin walls, valves, hold about 60-70% of blood volume
Arteries: thick, muscular, high pressure
Skeletal muscle pump plus valves drive venous return
d_4B_37.trap: Giving arterial properties (thick muscle, high pressure) to veins.
d_4B_37.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. Gas exchange is passive. O2 moves from high pressure (alveolus, 100 mmHg) to low pressure (blood, 40 mmHg) until the two are nearly equal.
Wrong. No pump is needed. The gradient already points into the blood. Trap: thinking all transport needs energy.
Wrong. This is backward. Gas moves from high partial pressure to low, and alveoli are higher here.
Wrong. At PO2 of 40 mmHg hemoglobin is only about 75% saturated, so it can still load more oxygen.

p: Each gas in a mixture has its own partial pressure, its share of the total pressure. A gas moves from where its partial pressure is high to where it is low.
In the lung, alveolar PO2 is about 100 and blood arriving is about 40, so oxygen flows into the blood. No energy is needed.

d_4B_40.eli: Water rolls downhill by itself. Oxygen rolls from the crowded air side to the empty blood side.
mem: Alveolar PO2 about 100; venous blood PO2 about 40
Gases diffuse passively down partial pressure gradients
Blood and alveolar PO2 nearly equalize in the capillary
d_4B_40.trap: Believing gas exchange needs active transport.

ox: Correct. Continuity says A1 x v1 = A2 x v2. If area is cut in half, speed must double so flow rate stays the same.
Wrong. This reverses the relationship. Smaller area gives faster flow, not slower.
Wrong. Quadrupling would come from cutting the radius in half, since area depends on r squared. Here the area, not the radius, is halved.
Wrong. Flow rate (volume per second) stays the same, so speed has to change when area changes.

p: For an incompressible fluid like blood, the same volume per second must pass through every section of the pipe. This volume per second is the flow rate.
Flow rate = area x speed. If area gets smaller, speed must get bigger to keep the flow rate the same.

q48.eli: Put your thumb over a garden hose end. The opening is smaller, so the water shoots out faster.
mem: A x v = constant
Area down means speed up
Area depends on radius squared: halve r, area becomes 1/4, speed becomes 4x

fm.f: A1 x v1 = A2 x v2, where A = cross-sectional area, v = flow speed (1 = before, 2 = after)
fm.s: A1 x v1 = (A1/2) x v2, so v2 = 2 x v1
fm.why: Flow rate is conserved in an incompressible fluid.
fm.nc: Half the area means double the speed.

q48.trap: Check whether the question gives area or radius. Halving radius quarters area.

ox: Correct. In Bernoulli's equation P + 1/2 x rho x v^2 stays constant in a horizontal pipe. Higher speed means a bigger kinetic term, so pressure must drop.
Wrong. This is the reverse. Faster flow in a horizontal pipe gives lower pressure.
Wrong. Speed changed, so the kinetic energy term changed. Pressure must change to keep the sum constant.
Wrong. Pressure falls but does not go to zero. The equation only trades pressure for kinetic energy.

p: Bernoulli's equation is energy conservation for a moving fluid. In a level pipe, the total of pressure plus the fluid's motion energy stays constant.
When the fluid speeds up (for example in a narrow section), its motion energy rises, so its pressure falls.

q49.eli: Pressure and speed share a fixed budget. Spend more on speed and you have less left for pressure.
mem: Horizontal pipe: P + 1/2 rho v^2 = constant
Narrow section: faster and lower pressure
Fast flow equals low pressure

fm.f: P + (1/2) x rho x v^2 = constant, where P = pressure, rho = fluid density, v = speed
fm.v: v increases from v1 to v2
fm.s: (1/2) x rho x v2^2 > (1/2) x rho x v1^2, so P2 < P1
fm.why: Height is the same, so only P and v can trade off.
fm.nc: No numbers; just compare direction.

q49.trap: Reversing the relationship: fast flow means low pressure, not high.

ox: Wrong. 20% is the part above the water. Trap: giving the leftover fraction instead of the submerged part.
Correct. A floating object displaces its own weight of fluid, so fraction submerged = density of object / density of fluid = 800/1000 = 80%.
Wrong. Fully submerged (100%) would mean equal density, like a neutral buoyancy object.
Wrong. It sinks only if denser than water. 800 is less than 1000, so it floats.

p: Buoyant force is the upward push from a fluid. It equals the weight of the fluid the object pushes aside.
A floating object is in balance: buoyant force equals its weight. That gives submerged fraction = density of object / density of fluid.

q50.eli: A boat sits lower in the water if it is heavier for its size. The more compact its material, the deeper it sinks.
mem: Floats if object density < fluid density
Fraction submerged = rho object / rho fluid
Equal density: fully submerged, suspended

fm.f: Fraction submerged = rho_obj / rho_fluid, where rho_obj = object density, rho_fluid = fluid density
fm.why: Floating means weight equals buoyant force, which gives this ratio.
fm.nc: Divide 800 by 1000 by moving a decimal.

q50.trap: Reporting the fraction above water (20%) instead of below.

ox: Wrong. 2x would be if flow scaled with radius. Poiseuille's law uses r to the fourth power.
Wrong. 4x is r squared, which is the area. Flow depends on r^4, not r^2.
Correct. Flow is proportional to r^4. Doubling r gives 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16 times more flow.
Wrong. 8x is r cubed. The exponent is 4 in Poiseuille's law.

p: Poiseuille's law gives the flow rate of a thick (viscous) fluid through a tube. Flow rises with pressure difference and radius, and falls with viscosity and length.
Radius is raised to the fourth power, so small changes in vessel radius create huge changes in flow. That is why vessel widening and narrowing control blood flow so strongly.

q51.eli: Making a straw twice as wide does not just double the milkshake you get. It gives you way more.
mem: Flow is proportional to r^4
Resistance is proportional to 1/r^4
Double r gives 16x flow; halve r gives 1/16 flow

fm.f: Q = (pi x dP x r^4) / (8 x eta x L), where Q = flow rate, dP = pressure difference, r = radius, eta = viscosity, L = length
fm.v: r goes to 2r; everything else constant
fm.why: Only r changes, so the ratio is just the radius ratio to the fourth power.

q51.trap: Using r squared (4) or r cubed (8) instead of r to the fourth.

ox: Correct. At constant volume and amount, P is proportional to T in kelvin. 600 K is twice 300 K, so pressure doubles.
Wrong. Heating raises pressure because molecules move faster and hit walls harder.
Wrong. The relationship is linear, not squared, so doubling T gives doubling, not quadrupling.
Wrong. The container is rigid, so volume cannot change to absorb it. Pressure must go up.

p: For a fixed amount of gas in a fixed volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature (Kelvin). Hotter gas molecules move faster and hit the walls harder.
Kelvin is the temperature scale starting at absolute zero. Always use it in gas laws, never Celsius.

q52.eli: A sealed balloon-like box with bouncing balls inside: heat them up, they hit the walls harder.
mem: Constant V and n: P/T = constant
Use Kelvin, K = C + 273
Double T in K means double P

fm.f: P1 / T1 = P2 / T2, where P = pressure, T = temperature in kelvin
fm.why: Volume and amount of gas are constant in a sealed rigid container.
fm.nc: 600/300 = 2, so pressure doubles.

q52.trap: Using Celsius. Going from 20 C to 40 C does not double the pressure.

ox: Wrong. More water per solute would dilute the urine and lower specific gravity toward 1.000. This is the opposite of what happened.
Wrong. Higher specific gravity means higher mass per volume, so the mass per volume went up, not down.
Correct. Specific gravity is density compared with water. The urine became more concentrated, so there is more dissolved solute (more mass) per volume.
Wrong. Anything with specific gravity above 1 is denser than water. 1.030 is denser, not less dense.

p: Specific gravity is the density of a substance divided by the density of water. It has no units. Water is exactly 1.000.
Urine with more dissolved waste and salts has more mass per volume, so a higher number. When you do not drink, the kidneys save water and the urine becomes more concentrated.

x4B_005.eli: A glass of salty water feels heavier than plain water. The more salt you add, the heavier each cupful.

Water = 1.000, above 1 is denser than water

fm.s: Higher SG means rho_urine is larger, so more solute per volume
fm.why: SG is a direct measure of density relative to water.

x4B_108.eli: If a pizza has one slice taken by an uninvited guest (water), everyone else shares the rest.
mem: PO2 = fraction x (Patm - 47).
Humidified inspired PO2 is about 150 mmHg.
Alveolar PO2 is about 100 mmHg.

fm.f: PO2 = FO2 x (Patm - PH2O), where FO2 = fraction of oxygen, Patm = total pressure, PH2O = water vapor pressure
fm.why: Water vapor takes part of the total pressure, so oxygen is a fraction of what remains.

x4B_108.sc: Round 713 to 700 and take one fifth: about 140-150, so pick 150.
x4B_108.trap: Ignoring water vapor (160) or subtracting 47 from the oxygen pressure instead of from the total.

ox: Wrong. Halving is the mole-fraction trap: O2's fraction of the mix halves, but you must multiply by the total pressure, which doubled.
Wrong. Helium is a separate gas. It does not react with or remove O2.
Wrong. Total pressure doubled, but that is the sum of all gases. The O2 itself did not change, so its own pressure did not either.
Correct. O2's moles, the container volume and the temperature are all unchanged, so P(O2) = nRT/V is unchanged. Helium only adds its own pressure.

p: Each gas in a mixture acts as if it were alone in the container. Its partial pressure (the pressure that one gas contributes) depends only on its own moles, the volume and the temperature.
Total pressure is just the sum of the partial pressures. Adding a new gas raises the total but does not change the others.

x4B_110.eli: Think of a classroom with 10 kids talking. Adding 10 new kids who talk makes the room louder overall, but the first 10 kids are not talking any louder.
mem: P(total) = P(gas 1) + P(gas 2) + ...
Partial pressure = mole fraction x total pressure
Adding an inert gas at constant V and T does not change other gases' partial pressures

fm.f: P = nRT/V, where P = pressure of one gas, n = its moles, R = gas constant, T = temperature, V = volume
fm.v: n(O2), T and V are all unchanged
fm.s: P(O2) = (same n)(R)(same T)/(same V) = same P
fm.why: The ideal gas law applies to each gas separately, and nothing in it changed for O2.
fm.nc: No calculation needed; just see that nothing in the formula changed.

x4B_110.trap: Students think doubling total pressure doubles every gas. Only the new gas adds pressure.

ox: Correct. Diffusion rate depends on the pressure gradient times solubility. CO2 is about 20 times more soluble than O2, so a 6 mmHg gradient does the work of a much larger one.
Wrong. Gas exchange in the lungs is passive diffusion down a gradient. No energy is used. This is the active-transport trap.
Wrong. CO2 (44 g/mol) is heavier than O2 (32 g/mol). Molar mass would make CO2 diffuse slower, not faster.
Wrong. Air has very little CO2 (about 0.04%), far less than O2. Partial pressure in air is lower, not higher.

concept.t: Why CO2 diffuses well with a small gradient
p: Gases cross the membrane by diffusion, moving from high to low partial pressure. How fast depends on the gradient and on how well the gas dissolves in the watery membrane (its solubility).
CO2 dissolves about 20 times better than O2. So a small gradient is enough.

x4B_116.eli: Two kids carry buckets across a bridge. One has a tiny hill to run down but a huge bucket, the other a steep hill but a small bucket. They deliver about the same amount.
mem: CO2 is about 20x more soluble than O2
Diffusion rate is proportional to (gradient x solubility)
Alveolar gas exchange is passive

fm.f: Rate is proportional to (P1 - P2) x S, where P1 - P2 = partial pressure gradient, S = solubility
fm.v: O2: gradient 60, S = 1 (reference). CO2: gradient 6, S = 20
fm.why: Fick's law says diffusion scales with both gradient and solubility.
fm.nc: Both products are easy mental multiplication.

ox: Wrong. Solubility is a constant for a given gas, liquid and temperature. It does not fall as pressure rises.
Wrong. Henry's law (dissolved gas is proportional to partial pressure) keeps working. The dissolved amount rises in a straight line.
Correct. Hemoglobin is about 98% full at 100 mmHg, so it can carry almost no more. Dissolved O2 rises linearly but stays small.
Wrong. High PO2 pushes O2 onto hemoglobin, not off it. Release happens at low PO2.

p: Most blood oxygen rides on hemoglobin (Hb), the protein in red blood cells. A small amount is dissolved in plasma. Dissolved O2 equals 0.003 mL per dL for each mmHg of PO2.
Hb is nearly saturated (full) at 100 mmHg. Extra pressure cannot fill it more, so only the small dissolved part grows.

mem: Hb is about 98% saturated at PaO2 100 mmHg
Dissolved O2 = 0.003 mL/dL per mmHg
Henry's law: dissolved gas is proportional to partial pressure

fm.f: Dissolved O2 = 0.003 x PaO2, where PaO2 = arterial O2 partial pressure in mmHg, answer in mL/dL
fm.why: This shows dissolved O2 grows linearly but stays tiny.
fm.nc: Move the decimal: 3 x 600 = 1800, then divide by 1000.

ox: Correct. Dissolved amount = solubility x partial pressure. CO2 is about 20x more soluble, so 20 x 40 = 800 beats 1 x 100 = 100.
Wrong. Equal concentrations would need equal solubility x pressure. These are 800 and 100 in relative units.
Wrong. Much CO2 becomes bicarbonate, but some always stays physically dissolved. This is the all-or-nothing trap.
Wrong. Higher PO2 alone does not decide it. You have to include solubility, and CO2's is far higher.

p: Henry's law says the amount of gas dissolved in a liquid equals the gas's solubility times its partial pressure. Solubility tells how well a gas dissolves in the liquid.
Two gases can have very different dissolved amounts at the same pressure because their solubilities differ.

mem: Dissolved gas = solubility x partial pressure
CO2 is about 20x more soluble than O2
Compare gases using both numbers, not pressure alone

fm.f: Dissolved amount is proportional to S x P, where S = relative solubility, P = partial pressure in mmHg
fm.why: Henry's law combines solubility and pressure.
fm.nc: 20 x 40 = 2 x 4 then add two zeros.

ox: Wrong. Lower viscosity would make flow bigger when pressure rises, not smaller. The gain fell, so this is backward.
Wrong. The tube is rigid, so the radius cannot grow. A wider tube would also increase flow.
Wrong. Poiseuille predicts doubling flow with doubling pressure. The high-pressure data did not double, so it fails there.
Correct. Turbulence wastes energy in eddies, so flow scales about with the square root of pressure. Doubling pressure gives about 1.4x flow, a 40% rise.

p: In laminar flow, fluid moves in smooth layers, and flow is proportional to pressure difference (Poiseuille's law). In turbulent flow, fluid swirls in eddies, which waste energy.
Turbulence appears at high speed. Then flow rises only with the square root of the pressure difference.

x4B_130.eli: Walking calmly down a hallway, pushing harder makes you go proportionally faster. In a crowded, chaotic hallway, pushing harder gets you far less extra speed.
mem: Laminar: Q is proportional to delta P
Turbulent: Q is proportional to square root of delta P
Turbulence is more likely at high velocity, large radius, low viscosity

fm.f: Turbulent: Q is proportional to sqrt(delta P), where Q = flow rate, delta P = pressure difference
fm.s: Q changes by sqrt(2), about 1.4, so flow rises about 40%
fm.why: A 40% gain matches the square-root rule.
fm.nc: Remember sqrt(2) is about 1.4.

x4B_130.trap: Assuming Poiseuille's law works at every pressure. It only holds for laminar flow.
